newsitem.title: USA: Gold supply seen weighing on demand - J.P. Morgan.
newsitem.headline: Gold supply seen weighing on demand - J.P. Morgan.

text.p: Rising gold mine output in the next 10 years may be enough to meet demand, limiting the potential for gains in gold prices, said J.P. Morgan vice president for commodities Kevin Crisp.
"I think that demand is going to be met in the future by more than adequate levels of supply," Crisp told the annual conference of Gold and Silver Institute.
Crisp showed the conference a chart projecting gold prices in a range of $330 to $380 an ounce to 2005.

"Quite clearly gold prices will trade over a wider range during the period, but the key point is that the price of gold may well trade in defined ranges for prolonged periods of time over the next 10 years," he said.
Gold mine output was forecast to rise to 2,700 to 2,900 tonnes by 2005 from 2,600 to 2,800 tonnes in 2000, 2,328 tonnes in 1996, and 2,135 tonnes in 1990, Crisp said.
Total supply, including scrap was forecast to rise to 3,950 to 4,550 tonnes in 2005 from 3,800 to 4,400 tonnes in 2000, 3,431 tonnes in 1996 and 3093 tonnes in 1990.

The largest expansions in gold mining are set to come from emerging markets, as exploration spending translates into new deposits in Latin America, Africa and Southeast Asia, while South African output will stabilize around the 500-tonne annual level, he said.

"Rising exploration spending, more overseas spending on exploration, increasingly freer markets, and improved or new funding and risk management structures strongly support our outlook for mine supply," he said.
"If my supply-side forecasts are realized, the burdens placed upon demand, and particularly the jewelry sector are going to grow substantially," he said.

Goldfields Mineral Services Ltd's (GFMS) annual survey showed annual world gold jewelry fabrication rose 28 percent between 1990 and 1996 and last year the jewelry industry consumed 460 tonnes more gold than was produced by the world's mines.

"There is, therefore, scope for rising mine output to be absorbed by consumers as along as other sources of supply are maintained at levels not far different to those seen on average in recent years," Crisp said.

"Demand growth to be maintained will require greater innovation in product development to meet changing consumer tastes and to compete for discretionary spending as consumer demand patterns for various goods and services change," he added. ((-Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 212-859-1640))
